passage: 'Vandana, you asked why I still keep that torn poster,' said Jomon Appachan, tapping the frame. 'I was fifteen, in Kottayam, and I thought school was a cage. Then one evening a travelling troupe performed a play in the church hall about a fisherman who taught his whole village to read. At the end he stood alone with a lamp and said, "A lamp does not ask if the room deserves it." I walked home in the dark, three kilometres, and did not feel my feet. That same night I started teaching our neighbour's boys their letters on the veranda. I did it for eleven years. That poster is from the play. It reminds me what being moved can make you do.'

qa.q: Where was the play performed?
qa.a: In the church hall.

qa.q: What does 'did not feel my feet' suggest about how young Jomon felt?
qa.a: He was so deeply moved by the play that he was lost in the feeling and barely noticed the long walk.

qa.q: How could Vandana use a moment of inspiration like this?
qa.a: Vandana could turn it into one small, regular action right away, the way Jomon began teaching letters that same night.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's boys have been affected?
qa.a: They got years of free lessons, so the play's message reached them through Jomon.

grounding: Shows a teenager deeply moved by a piece of theatre and its idea, turning the feeling into lasting action.

passage: Chinmay had saved sixty rupees for the bus to the district town, where a retired forest guard was speaking at the college hall about thirty years of protecting elephants. Halfway there, the bus broke down in the rain. His friend Bhupen wanted to turn back. 'We'll miss half of it.' 'Then we'll hear half,' Chinmay said, and they walked the last four kilometres under one umbrella. They slipped in, soaked, for the final twenty minutes. She was describing sitting all night beside a wounded calf, refusing to leave. Chinmay stopped shivering. Afterwards he pushed to the front and asked, voice cracking, how someone like him could start. She wrote the name of a nature club in his wet notebook. On the walk back he talked the whole way; Bhupen barely got a word in.

qa.q: How much had Chinmay saved for the bus?
qa.a: Sixty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay stop shivering during the talk?
qa.a: He was so absorbed and moved by her story that he forgot the cold.

qa.q: What should Chinmay do next to keep this feeling alive?
qa.a: Contact the nature club soon and go to a meeting, perhaps with Bhupen, before the excitement fades.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have experienced the day?
qa.a: Probably tired and a little bored by the long walk, but Bhupen could see how much the talk lit up Chinmay.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager so moved by a role model that he pushes through rain and a breakdown to hear her.

passage: The chemistry exam was at nine the next morning, and Devika had read the same page on bonds four times. Her phone lay face-down, but she kept flipping it over to check whether the senior from the quiz club had replied to her 'good luck for the finals' message. He hadn't. In her head he was already perfect: kind to juniors, brilliant, the sort who would remember her birthday. She had spoken to him exactly twice. At ten, Sunaina called to revise. 'Are you even listening?' 'Sorry. Do you think he's the type who reads messages and doesn't reply?' Sunaina sighed. 'Dev, you don't know what type he is. You know his profile picture.' Devika laughed, a little hurt. Then she put the phone in the kitchen and opened the page on bonds again.

qa.q: How many times had Devika spoken to the senior?
qa.a: Exactly twice.

qa.q: What does Devika imagining him as perfect suggest about her crush?
qa.a: Her feelings are built more on her own idealised picture than on actually knowing him.

qa.q: What small step helped Devika at the end, and why?
qa.a: Putting the phone in the kitchen, because it stopped the constant checking so she could study.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see Devika's crush?
qa.a: Sunaina sees it as based on very little real knowledge and gently teases her back toward reality.

grounding: Shows a teenager's idealised crush crowding out exam revision the night before a test.

passage: Every day that week, Parul took the long way home through the Jaipur market, past the library where the boy with the sketchbook sat by the window. She had never heard his voice. She had decided he was gentle, that he drew his grandmother, that he probably liked old songs. She filled the back pages of her notebook with his initials beside hers, then scribbled them out. On Friday, Noor walked with her. 'Parul, this is twenty minutes extra. For a window.' 'You don't get it.' 'Try me.' Parul stopped. 'When I think about him, everything else goes quiet.' Noor softened. Then they reached the library. The window seat was empty. Parul's stomach dropped, and the whole walk home she barely spoke.

qa.q: In which city is the market?
qa.a: Jaipur.

qa.q: What did Parul mean by 'everything else goes quiet'?
qa.a: Thinking about the boy gives her an intense, absorbing feeling that crowds out her other worries.

qa.q: How could Noor support Parul without mocking her?
qa.a: Noor could keep walking with Parul sometimes, listen, and gently help her notice how much she has imagined compared with what she knows. 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Parul actually spoke to the boy?
qa.a: Her idealised picture would meet the real person, which might disappoint or surprise her, but it would be real.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's intense, idealised crush on a boy she has never spoken to.

passage: Class teacher's note, Wednesday. Divyansh, usually first to answer, has not raised his hand since Monday. Today he sat by the window with his hood up in the heat and left his lunch unopened. His friends told me, carefully, that he had asked Zainab to go to the school fair with him and she had said no in front of a few people. Zainab looked uncomfortable too and has been sitting at the other end of the room. At break I asked Divyansh to help me carry books to the staffroom. On the stairs he said, 'It's stupid. It feels like my chest is full of stones.' I told him it wasn't stupid. Next step: I have let his parents know he's having a hard week and mentioned the counsellor's hours to him; I'll check in on Friday. I'll also speak quietly with Zainab so she doesn't feel blamed.

qa.q: What did Divyansh leave unopened?
qa.a: His lunch.

qa.q: What does 'my chest is full of stones' reveal about Divyansh?
qa.a: It shows he is in real, heavy pain from the rejection, even though he calls it stupid.

qa.q: Why was asking him to carry books a good move?
qa.a: It gave him a private, low-pressure moment to talk without being singled out in class.

qa.q: How might Zainab be feeling this week?
qa.a: She seems uncomfortable, perhaps awkward about how the no happened, even though she was free to say no.

grounding: Shows a teenager overwhelmed by the pain of a public romantic rejection, noticed and supported by a teacher.

passage: Saturday, late. Chinmay's birthday was today. I found out from the photos. Seven of them at the new cafe near the station, all from his coaching batch, cake on his face. Last year it was just us two on my terrace with samosas. He didn't even tell me there was a plan. I keep opening the photo and closing it. My whole body feels heavy, like after a fever, and I snapped at Amma when she asked if I'd eaten. I'm not angry at her. I don't even know if I'm angry at him. Maybe I'm just not his best friend anymore and nobody told me. Tomorrow I'll go for a long cycle ride early. Maybe I'll tell Amma. Maybe. – Ramesh

qa.q: Where was Chinmay's birthday celebrated this year?
qa.a: At the new cafe near the station.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh snap at Amma?
qa.a: Ramesh was hurting from being left out and the pain spilled onto Amma, though Ramesh says it isn't anger at her.

qa.q: What would you advise Ramesh for tomorrow?
qa.a: Go on the ride and then talk to Amma or someone Ramesh trusts; later Ramesh could ask Chinmay honestly what changed.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see this if Ramesh told him?
qa.a: Chinmay may not have realised how much leaving Ramesh out hurt, and might feel sorry or awkward.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's acute pain at being dropped by a best friend.

passage: I'm Damini, and I sit behind Yogesh in the Friday circle our class teacher runs. Usually he makes jokes when it's his turn. This Friday he didn't. He stared at the floor for a long time, and his leg kept bouncing. Then he said his father lost his job two months ago and that he's been pretending everything is normal because he didn't want anyone feeling sorry for him. His voice went thin at the end. Nobody laughed. I didn't know what to do, so I just said, 'Thanks for telling us.' A couple of others nodded. At lunch he sat with us instead of on the back bench. He seemed lighter, or maybe just tired. I'm honestly not sure which.

qa.q: How long ago did Yogesh's father lose his job?
qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: What might Yogesh's bouncing leg suggest before he spoke?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous about the risk of telling the class something so personal.

qa.q: How could the class teacher support Yogesh after this?
qa.a: The teacher could check in with him privately, thank him for trusting the group, and keep the circle a place where no one mocks what is shared.

qa.q: How does Damini see the change in Yogesh at lunch?
qa.a: Damini notices he seems lighter or tired, but admits not being sure what he feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of dropping his joking cover to share something painful with classmates.

passage:
Monday: Chaitanya typed 'can we talk?' to Shalini and deleted it three times. For months he had been pretending the move to the new school was easy. It wasn't. He ate lunch in the library most days.
Wednesday: On the steps after tuition, he finally said it. 'I'm not okay here. I don't really have anyone except you.' His ears burned. Shalini didn't laugh. She was quiet, then said, 'I thought you didn't need anyone. You always seem so sorted.'
Saturday: She texted him a photo of a chess club notice: 'I'll come to the first one with you 🙂'. He saved the photo. For the first time in weeks, he didn't dread Monday.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya eat lunch most days?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya's ears burn when he spoke?
qa.a: He felt exposed and embarrassed, since admitting he wasn't okay was a big emotional risk.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya's openness pay off, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Shalini listened without laughing; next he could go to chess club with her and keep telling her honestly how things are.

qa.q: How did Shalini's picture of Chaitanya change?
qa.a: She had thought he was sorted and didn't need anyone, and learned he was actually lonely.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager moving from hiding loneliness to risking honesty with a friend, and what followed.

passage: Thursday, 11 pm. Prelims start Monday, and today in the maths revision test my hands went cold and my brain just stopped. Couldn't even read question 3. Sunaina saw me and did that thing from our PT class: pointed at her own chest and breathed slowly in and out, like a slow balloon. I copied her. Four breaths, maybe five. The numbers came back. Didn't finish, but I did most of it. Tonight I couldn't sleep, so I went up and down our building stairs three times, fast, till my legs burned, and then did the balloon breathing on my bed. Heart's slower now. Writing this down so I remember it works. Maybe I'll ask Sir if we can practise this before Monday. – Kamal

qa.q: What did Sunaina do to help Kamal during the test?
qa.a: She pointed at her chest and breathed slowly in and out.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when Kamal's hands went cold during the test?
qa.a: Kamal felt panicked and frozen, so anxious that reading the question became impossible.

qa.q: What would you add to Kamal's plan before Monday?
qa.a: Practise the breathing daily while calm so it comes easily in the exam, and tell a teacher or parent if the panic keeps coming.

qa.q: What was it like for Sunaina to see Kamal freeze?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt worried for Kamal and quickly thought of a quiet way to help without drawing attention. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager using slow breathing and physical exercise to calm exam anxiety.

passage:
Kalyani: debate finals in 30 min and my hands are literally shaking 😰
Akash: ok where are u
Kalyani: backstage corner. everyone's so loud
Akash: go out to the corridor. walk up and down twice
Kalyani: ok walking
Akash: now breathe out longer than in. like blowing on hot chai
Kalyani: this feels so silly
Akash: silly but it works for me before races
Kalyani: ok 3 times done. shoulders came down from my ears lol
Akash: now shake out your hands. like flicking water
Kalyani: done. still nervous but i can think
Akash: nervous is fine. frozen isn't
Kalyani: ok going in. thank u 🙏
Akash: go get them 👍

qa.q: Where was Kalyani waiting before the finals?
qa.a: In a backstage corner.

qa.q: What does 'shoulders came down from my ears' suggest about how Kalyani was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Kalyani's body had been tense with anxiety and the walking and breathing were helping Kalyani relax.

qa.q: Which of Akash's suggestions could Kalyani keep using, and why?
qa.a: The long out-breath and shaking out the hands, because they are quick and quiet and helped Kalyani think clearly again.

qa.q: How might Akash feel reading 'thank u'?
qa.a: Glad and a little proud that tricks from Akash's own races helped a friend.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager using walking, longer out-breaths and shaking out tension to manage stage nerves.

passage: 'So, Bhavna, you asked when I started questioning stuff. Honestly? Class 11. Our school had this rule that the girls' section cleaned the labs after practicals while the boys went straight to games. Nobody asked why. I asked Sir once and he said, "Francis, it's always been like that." That answer bugged me for weeks. Like, is something right just because it's old? Then it got messier. My friend broke a beaker and a girl got blamed, and if I told the truth, he'd get the fine. I stayed quiet for two days and felt disgusting. On day three I told. He didn't talk to me for a month. I'd do it again, but I still don't think it was simple.'

qa.q: Who cleaned the labs after practicals under the old rule?
qa.a: The girls' section.

qa.q: How did Francis feel during the two days of staying quiet?
qa.a: Francis felt disgusted, torn between loyalty to a friend and fairness to the girl being blamed.

qa.q: What could Francis try to get the cleaning rule changed?
qa.a: Francis could raise it respectfully with the class teacher or student council, asking for a reason and suggesting a shared rota.

qa.q: How might the girl who was blamed see Francis's choice?
qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and relieved that someone told the truth for her.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning a rule kept only by habit and struggling with a loyalty-versus-fairness dilemma.

passage: I'm Simran. My brother Jagdish is sixteen, and last Sunday he did something I'm still thinking about. When Kamla didi, who helps with the cooking, finished, Dadi handed her tea in the steel cup kept separately on the top shelf, like always. Jagdish took his own glass, poured tea into it, and handed that to Kamla didi instead. Nobody spoke. Dadi's face went stiff. Later I heard him on the balcony with Papa, asking, 'If we'd be hurt by this, why is it okay for her?' Papa didn't have an answer, only 'Dadi grew up differently.' Jagdish said, 'I know. I'm not angry at Dadi. I just can't do it anymore.' I don't know if he was scared. His hands were shaking a little when he poured.

qa.q: Where was the separate steel cup kept?
qa.a: On the top shelf.

qa.q: What might Jagdish's shaking hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was nervous, knowing that breaking the family habit might upset Dadi, even though he felt sure it was wrong.

qa.q: How could Papa support both Jagdish and Dadi?
qa.a: He could talk with Dadi gently and privately, respecting her, while making clear the family can change the habit.

qa.q: What might this moment have been like for Kamla didi?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised, awkward or quietly respected, though Simran, telling it, can't know for sure.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager challenging an unfair household custom and defining his own sense of right, seen by his sibling.

passage: In the school bus queue, three boys from the cricket team had surrounded Sachin again. 'S-s-sachin, s-say your name,' one of them sang, and the others laughed. Farida, fifteen, felt her stomach drop. Those boys were friends with everyone she wanted to be friends with. She had watched this happen twice already and said nothing. This time she stepped out of the line. 'Stop it. It's not funny.' Her voice came out smaller than she wanted. One of them rolled his eyes. 'Relax, it's a joke.' 'Then laugh at yourselves.' She stood beside Sachin until the bus came. On board, a girl she barely knew moved her bag so Farida could sit. Later that week Farida heard she was being called 'the preachy one.' She told the class teacher what had happened anyway.

qa.q: How many times had Farida watched this happen before?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did Farida's stomach drop before she spoke?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing standing, since the boys were friends with people she wanted to be close to.

qa.q: Why was Farida's later step, telling the teacher, important?
qa.a: It brought in an adult who can stop the bullying for Sachin, instead of leaving it to one brave moment.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Farida stood beside him?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, though maybe also embarrassed to be the centre of attention. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager defending a bullied classmate despite the social cost, then involving a teacher.

passage:
Dear Lalit,
I know you're angry that I showed the group chat to Ma'am. I'm writing because you won't pick up my calls. I didn't do it to get you in trouble. When the edited photos of the new boy started, I laughed at the first one. Then someone wrote that he should just leave the school. He's been absent three days since. I kept thinking, what if that was my little brother? I know everyone's calling me a snitch. Two people have left me on read all week. It's awful, honestly. But I'd rather lose some friends than watch someone get pushed out. You were never one of the people making them. I hope you'll talk to me.
Kashish

qa.q: How many days has the new boy been absent?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What does Kashish mean by 'It's awful, honestly'?
qa.a: Kashish is hurt by being called a snitch and ignored, so the social cost weighs heavily even though Kashish stands by the choice.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if the teasing of Kashish continues?
qa.a: Tell a teacher or parent and lean on supportive friends, while staying calm and not hitting back.

qa.q: How might Lalit see this letter?
qa.a: Lalit may still be angry but could soften, since Kashish says Lalit wasn't one of those making the photos and wants to stay friends.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager reporting online bullying of a classmate and bearing the unpopularity that followed.

passage: 'You ask big questions at night, Sunaina, just like I did,' said Darshan Dada, settling his shawl. 'At sixteen I used to sleep on the roof in summer, and I would look at the stars and feel very small. What is all this for? Why am I here and not some other boy? I asked the priest at our temple, and he gave me one answer. I asked my science teacher, and she gave me another. I asked my friend the potter, who never went to school, and he said, "I don't know. But when I shape a pot, I feel joined to something." I kept all three answers for years. I still don't have just one. But I stopped being afraid of the question. It kept me company.'

qa.q: Where did young Darshan sleep in summer?
qa.a: On the roof.

qa.q: How did young Darshan feel looking at the stars?
qa.a: He felt very small and full of questions about why he existed.

qa.q: What could Sunaina take from how Darshan Dada handled these questions?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask different trusted people, keep their answers, and let the question be company rather than something scary.

qa.q: How does the potter's answer differ from the other two?
qa.a: It comes from feeling and daily work rather than teaching or scripture, showing meaning can be found in doing.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of existence by gathering spiritual, scientific and personal answers.

passage: Yamini had planned the sunrise walk with Ritu for weeks, but at five Ritu texted that she had a fever and couldn't come. Yamini went up the hill behind the town alone. Fog swallowed the view; there would be no sunrise. She sat on the wet bench anyway, annoyed, hood up. Lately every question in her head ended the same way: what is the point of any of it, marks, college, even being kind? Her family prayed every evening; her best friend believed in nothing she could name. Yamini didn't know where she stood. In the fog she could hear a temple bell below, a dog, someone's pressure cooker. For one strange second she felt part of all of it. She typed to Ritu: 'No sunrise. But something. Tell you later.'

qa.q: Why couldn't Ritu come on the walk?
qa.a: She had a fever.

qa.q: What did Yamini feel for 'one strange second' in the fog?
qa.a: She felt connected to everything around her, a sense of belonging her questions hadn't given her.

qa.q: What might help Yamini keep exploring these questions?
qa.a: Talking them over with Ritu, her family or a teacher she trusts, and reading different views, without rushing to settle on one.

qa.q: How might Ritu react to the message 'No sunrise. But something'?
qa.a: She would probably be curious and a bit sorry she missed it, and keen to hear what Yamini meant.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager wrestling with questions of purpose and glimpsing a feeling of universal connection on a foggy morning.

passage: Last year I thought volunteering meant weekend photos at a tree-planting drive. Then I noticed that Manoj, who uses a wheelchair, never came to library period. The library was on the second floor, and our school has no lift. Everyone knew; nobody did anything, including me, for two years. I asked him if he minded me raising it. He said, 'Go ahead, Ankita, but don't make me a poster.' So I didn't. I got twenty classmates to sign a request, met the principal with Manoj, and we offered to run a book trolley on the ground floor every Wednesday ourselves. It's been eight months. I still run it. What changed in me is that I stopped looking for causes far away.

qa.q: Which floor was the library on?
qa.a: The second floor.

qa.q: What did Manoj mean by 'don't make me a poster'?
qa.a: He wanted the problem fixed without being turned into a symbol or pity story; he cared about his dignity.

qa.q: What did Ankita get right in taking up the issue?
qa.a: Ankita asked Manoj first, respected his wish, and offered practical help instead of only complaining.

qa.q: How might other students benefit from the trolley?
qa.a: They also get easy access to books on the ground floor, and see that small changes can include everyone.

grounding: Shows a teenager directing their energy into service by standing up for a classmate who was being left out.

passage: Volunteer coordinator's note, Sunday community kitchen, week six. Zubin arrived early again, before the dal was on. He has stopped asking what to do and now checks the rota himself. Today an elderly man was turned away at the gate by another volunteer because he had no token. Zubin went after him, brought him back, and asked me quietly whether we could keep five extra plates for people without tokens. Yusuf, who helps with serving, backed him up. Zubin was polite but firm. I agreed to try it for a month. Next step: I will ask Zubin and Yusuf to write the new rule on the board and explain it to the other volunteers themselves, so it doesn't feel like a favour.

qa.q: How many extra plates did Zubin ask to keep?
qa.a: Five extra plates.

qa.q: Why did Zubin go after the elderly man?
qa.a: He seemed troubled that someone in need was turned away over a token, and wanted to fix it rather than just feel bad.

qa.q: Why is asking the boys to explain the new rule a good step?
qa.a: It gives them ownership and helps other volunteers understand the reason instead of seeing it as special treatment.

qa.q: How might the volunteer who turned the man away feel?
qa.a: Perhaps embarrassed or defensive, since they were following the token rule; a clear explanation may help them accept the change.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager committed to volunteering who speaks up for people left out by a rule, seen by a coordinator.

passage: At the district basketball match in the club gym, a girl from the other team elbowed Jahnavi hard in the ribs under the basket. The referee missed it. Jahnavi's face went hot, and she spun round, ready to shove back. Gautam, her team's assistant coach, was shouting something from the bench, but she couldn't hear it over the crowd. Then she saw the scoreboard: two fouls already against her name. One more and she'd sit out the final quarter. She unclenched her fists, turned her back, and jogged to her position, breathing out hard. At the timeout, Gautam said, 'I thought you'd swing.' 'I almost did,' she said, still shaking. 'Then I did the maths.'

qa.q: How many fouls did Jahnavi already have?
qa.a: Two fouls.

qa.q: What does 'I almost did' show about Jahnavi's state in that moment?
qa.a: She was flooded with anger and close to shoving back, and only just caught herself.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi cool her choice, and how could she practise it?
qa.a: Looking at the scoreboard gave her a reason to pause; she could practise a set cue, like one breath and a glance, for heated moments.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt watching from the bench?
qa.a: Worried she would retaliate, then relieved and proud when she held back.

grounding: Shows a teenager catching herself in a moment of hot anger and choosing with a cooler head.

passage:
Dear Sudha Aunty,
You told me to write when something happened that I didn't want to tell Ammi yet, so here it is. On Saturday some boys from my building were daring each other to race scooters down the flyover ramp without helmets. They'd filmed two already and everyone was screaming. It was my turn. My heart was banging and I actually had my hand on the handle. Then I remembered what you said about deciding things 'before the crowd arrives.' I'd already decided, weeks ago: no dares on roads. So I said, 'Not doing it. I'll film.' They called me scared. I was, a bit. But I'd rather be scared on the pavement. I'll tell Ammi this weekend.
Tanvir

qa.q: What had Tanvir decided weeks ago?
qa.a: No dares on roads.

qa.q: What do Tanvir's banging heart and hand on the handle suggest Tanvir was feeling?
qa.a: Tanvir was caught up in the excitement and pressure and was close to going along with it.

qa.q: What lesson from this could help Tanvir in future heated moments?
qa.a: Deciding limits calmly in advance, so Tanvir has a ready answer when the crowd and excitement hit.

qa.q: How might Sudha Aunty feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Relieved Tanvir was safe, proud that her advice helped, and glad Tanvir plans to tell Ammi. 🙏

grounding: Illustrates a teenager resisting a risky dare under peer pressure by relying on a decision made in a calm moment.
